#134399. Movement can change how quickly you learn from the same visual clues

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1040 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Movement can change how quickly you learn from the same visual clues

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1040 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a virtual reality study, swinging a lightsaber or throwing a punch helped volunteers learn visual patterns that required combining two features.
  • In the textbook account, learning happens in the head, and the hands do nothing more than report the answer.
  • Volunteers learned to sort striped discs more accurately when they answered by swinging a virtual lightsaber or punching a virtual target.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a virtual reality study, swinging a lightsaber or throwing a punch helped volunteers learn visual patterns that required combining two features.

In the textbook account, learning happens in the head, and the hands do nothing more than report the answer.

Volunteers learned to sort striped discs more accurately when they answered by swinging a virtual lightsaber or punching a virtual target.

The advantage appeared when they had to judge the angle and thickness of the stripes together.

In the punching experiment, volunteers kept their lead when they switched to button presses immediately after training.

For sorting tasks that could be solved with explicit rules, bigger movements gave volunteers no clear advantage.

Luke Rosedahl is an assistant professor of biomedical engineering in Florida Atlantic University‘s College of Engineering and Computer Science.

Professor Rosedahl conducted the experiments at Brown University with Yuka Sasaki and Takeo Watanabe.

The 160 participants were young adults recruited around Brown, sorting striped discs in a headset, so how far the result reaches outside a lab is still open.

“We found that larger movements substantially improved learning when people had to recognize patterns by integrating multiple features, but provided no meaningful benefit when people learned categories using explicit rules,” Rosedahl noted.

In a recent development, “Even more intriguing, the benefit occurred whether participants swung at the target or punched a separate response box. The movement itself appeared to matter, not whether it directly interacted with what they were learning.”.

Some categories come with a rule. If it has whiskers and meows, it’s a cat. Psychologists call these rule-based categories, and people learn them by testing hypotheses, which is thought to lean on the front of the brain.

In a recent development, other categories can’t be put into words. A radiologist’s sense that a lesion looks aggressive comes from weighing several features at once, and so does a driver’s read on whether a road is icy.

People learn these by comparing each new case with ones they’ve seen.

That kind of learning is thought to run through the striatum, a deep brain structure tied to movement and habits.

Both kinds were tested with the same material: gray discs striped at different angles and thicknesses, shown one at a time in a virtual reality hallway.

In a recent development, for the rule-based version, thickness and angle could be judged separately. For the other version, the dividing line ran diagonally through both, so no single feature gave the answer.

Sources indicate that in the first experiment, 80 people each sorted 600 discs into two groups over 12 blocks, with the disc flashing green or red after every answer. Half answered by pulling a controller trigger.

The other half swung a virtual lightsaber and hit the disc.

On the hard, no-rule categories, the swingers pulled ahead by the second block and stayed ahead for most of the session.

On the rule-based categories, the swingers did very slightly worse, by an amount that could have been chance.

A swing takes longer than a button press, and it touches the thing being judged. Either could have been the real cause.

In a second experiment with 80 fresh volunteers, some punched a virtual response box separate from the disc, while others pulled a controller trigger.

Every disc stayed on screen for 2.5 seconds, however quickly they answered.

The rule-based task was also made harder, with two rules to discover instead of one, in case the first version had simply been too easy to show a difference.

Punching still helped on the no-rule categories and still did nothing for the rule-based ones. Slower answers went with worse accuracy, not better, so taking extra time wasn’t the reason.

In the final 100 training trials of the task that required combining both features, volunteers who punched got 90.7% of answers right, compared with 81.0% for those who pressed a button.

Then everyone switched. The punchers moved to buttons and scored 89.5%, almost unchanged. The button group moved to punching and scored 83.1%.

Whatever the big movements had built was still there when the movement stopped, which points to better learning rather than a boost at the moment of answering.

According to recent reports, the authors can’t say what the arm is doing for the brain, and they said so. They offered two possibilities.

One possibility is that more effortful movements increase dopamine release in the striatum, which could help reinforce learning.

Effortful actions have also been shown to steer attention toward the features that matter. And movement has helped in other corners of learning, the authors wrote, such as writing by hand to learn to recognize letters.

The selectivity is the clue. If swinging had simply made people more engaged, Rosedahl’s team wrote, both kinds of categories should have improved.

The benefit appeared only when people had to combine visual features, a kind of learning thought to involve motor circuits.

The result also raises a question about decades of earlier work, nearly all of it done with button presses.

Those studies found that no-rule categories are learned slowly and that written instructions on how to perform them don’t help.

The authors suggested that the buttons themselves may have been holding that learning back.

The team didn’t record which hand participants favored, and controllers were handed out in no particular order, so the role of handedness and motor experience is unmeasured.

In a recent development, other category types, such as rules with exceptions, may respond differently. And everything happened with participants seated and a headset on.

The team wrote that the next studies should test the effect in real training, in fields such as radiology and aviation.

There, the judgments that can’t be put into words are the ones that take years to learn. Rosedahl framed the stakes in one line.

“Incorporating movement could offer a simple way to improve learning in situations where conventional approaches fall short,” he said.

Whether a bigger swing of the arm can speed up a radiologist’s eye, and not only a student’s sorting of striped discs, is the test that comes next.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

Prickly pear cacti generate electricity, and sunlight changes their voltage

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1030 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Prickly pear cacti generate a small voltage that varies with sunlight, and researchers are exploring whether it could power field sensors.
  • In a California greenhouse, a row of prickly pear cacti is quietly generating electricity.
  • When eight stems were wired together, they reached 4.5 volts, three times the voltage of a standard AA battery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prickly pear cacti generate a small voltage that varies with sunlight, and researchers are exploring whether it could power field sensors.

In a California greenhouse, a row of prickly pear cacti is quietly generating electricity. A single stem can produce about half a volt.

When eight stems were wired together, they reached 4.5 volts, three times the voltage of a standard AA battery.

The trick depends on the unusual way cacti photosynthesize. They store up acid overnight and use it up in daylight.

That turns each stem into something like a small living solar panel.

The work was led by the University of California, Santa Cruz (UCSC).

Most plants take in carbon dioxide during the day. They open tiny pores in their leaves, let the gas in and use sunlight to turn it into sugar.

Sources indicate that the downside is that water escapes through those open pores. In a desert, that’s a costly trade.

Sources indicate that prickly pears and some of their relatives work around this problem. Aloe, pineapple, and dragon fruit use a system called crassulacean acid metabolism, or CAM for short.

According to recent reports, these plants keep their pores closed in the heat of the day and open them in the cool of the night. They pull in carbon dioxide while it’s dark and store it as malic acid, the same acid that makes green apples sour.

When the sun comes up, they break the acid down and finish making sugar.

It has been revealed that the cactus’s shape provides the second part of the trick. Prickly pear stems are thick and opaque, another way of holding on to water, so photosynthesis happens only in the outer two millimeters or so.

When morning light hits one side of a stem, that side starts using up its stored acid. The shaded side keeps its acid.

The result is a difference in acidity across the stem, from one face to the other. That difference creates a voltage, and the researchers tap into it with a wired electrode inserted into the plant.

In effect, the cactus charges overnight and releases the energy during the day.

The idea came from Michael Loik, a professor of environmental studies who has studied cactus physiology and ecology for about 40 years.

“I’ve been obsessed with the plant since forever, it seems,” Loik remarked.

He suspected the cacti could produce electricity. He and Charlie Chesney, then a PhD student in environmental studies, set out to prove it and measure it.

According to recent reports, they used cacti in field plots at the UCSC Farm, in greenhouses, and in the lab. Chesney recruited a large group of undergraduates from engineering, the sciences, and the social sciences, and seven of them are now authors on the paper.

“The undergraduate students told me they liked this project so much because it felt whimsical, and like a light-hearted approach to something that is so serious,” noted Chesney, who led the project.

“It was a fun way to explore climate solutions that put creativity first.”.

When researchers wired eight stems together, they measured 4.5 volts, three times the nominal voltage of a standard AA battery.

The researchers are exploring whether prickly pears could power low-energy field sensors. The voltage may also help growers monitor how the plants respond to changing conditions.

Chesney has since graduated. Colleen Josephson, an assistant professor of electrical and computer engineering, is continuing the work with her PhD student John Madden, and they are looking for ways to strengthen the signal.

The team also wanted to know how weather and growing conditions affect the voltage. The cacti behaved very much like solar panels.

Voltage was much higher in summer than in winter, and through the day it tracked the amount of sunlight.

“Just how closely the voltage aligned with the sunlight conditions was really surprising,” Chesney stated.

“Comparing winter to summer voltage, the voltage really follows the same pattern of the amount of sunlight throughout the day.”.

There is an upper limit. Too much sunlight and the cactus goes into self-protection mode.

Sources indicate that “If it’s too high, then the cactus will start trying to protect itself from a sunburn, which will also decrease the voltage,” Chesney stated. “There’s a balance, a mid-range of light that causes the voltage to be higher.”.

In a recent development, then came the drought test. The team stopped watering some cacti for 15 months.

The plants survived and kept photosynthesizing. Sometimes, they even produced more voltage than cacti that had been watered normally.

“This was a really surprising result, but also indicated how resilient a cactus is – it could still produce electricity even when it seems, to us, like it’s near death,” Chesney said.

A separate experiment led by undergraduate Erin Langness looked at nitrogen, a common fertilizer ingredient.

Nitrogen increased the cacti’s store of malic acid, so they kept photosynthesizing and producing voltage later into the day.

According to recent reports, the team isn’t trying to run homes on cacti. They have something smaller in mind.

The researchers are exploring whether prickly pears could power low-energy field sensors.

As climate change puts more pressure on crops, farmers increasingly use low-power sensors to monitor their fields.

The voltage may also help growers monitor how the plants respond to changing conditions.

That could be useful on farms that grow prickly pears for their edible pads, called nopales, and their fruit, called tunas.

“There are many commercial applications of cacti where monitoring their health using a low-power system like ours, that is just operating off on the side and is self-powered,” Loik said.

“This could be a really interesting avenue to pursue. It could be connected to a plant that acts as sentinel, measuring conditions and sending it back to the base station at the farmer’s office.”.

Other CAM plants, such as agave and pineapple, might work too. The researchers note, however, that some of them may not tolerate the wires as well as the prickly pear does.

The study is published in the journal Plants, People, Planet.

  • A draft resolution that Massie read aloud on the House floor on Monday accused Hegseth of eight violations of law or the Constitution, including that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., conducts a news conference outside the Capitol on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., took to the House floor Monday to unveil a resolution that would impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and a vote on the glitch could occur by Wednesday.

A draft resolution that Massie read aloud on the House floor on Monday accused Hegseth of eight violations of law or the Constitution, including that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Massie's resolution also charges Hegseth with disregarding protection of civilians in wartime and suppressing the free speech of a U.S. senator.

Massie confirmed his intention to file the resolution as a matter of the privileges of the House.

Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., will now have to rule as to whether the resolution constitutes a proper question of the privileges of the House. There is precedent from prior instances when impeachment was found to be valid as it relates to the House’s constitutionally granted powers.

He must schedule a vote to occur within two legislative days. Assuming that the speaker rules that Massie's resolution is privileged, the House could vote on the resolution itself, or on a motion to table it or refer it to committee.

It has been revealed that if the House were to impeach Hegseth under this process, it would mark a historical anomaly. According to the Congressional Research Service, recent attempts to impeach an official as a matter of the privileges of the House have not resulted in approval of the resolution. In cases in which an official has been impeached, the House has nearly always chosen to conduct an investigation first.

Industry observers note that in an interview on Oct. 26, Massie put the chances of his resolution being adopted at 50-50.

In comments to reporters outside the Capitol after his floor remarks, Massie said he suspected some Republicans may back his resolution but he indicated he has neither asked for nor received any such assurances from any of them.

He predicted there could be some GOP support in the Senate if Hegseth is impeached and it goes to trial. He noted that if the trial does not start until 2027, any Republicans who might vote to convict Hegseth would presumably be joined by most if not all of a more sizeable Senate Democratic caucus.

According to recent reports, massie's odds of success for his resolution may now be greater than his previous 50-50 prediction given the results of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which gave Democrats control over both chambers in the next Congress — a vote motivated largely by opposition to the Iran war and its inflationary impact.

The questions now are, first, how many House Republicans will defy President Donald Trump and vote to impeach Hegseth; and, secondly, how many incumbents who lost their reelection bids on Nov. 3, a cohort that is disproportionately Republican, might be absent for the impeachment vote?

Massie stated some Republicans who lost their reelection bids may feel freer to vote to impeach Hegseth. And he also said Republicans who were reelected and will have to face voters in 2028 may also think about how their vote on an impeachment resolution would reverberate politically.

"It's going to be everybody's conscience, and then they'll have to live with that vote," Massie said. "And they're going to have to live with that vote two years from now if they're not part of the retirement caucus. And if they were part of the retirement caucus, what do they have to lose?".

Asked why he did not bring articles of impeachment against President Donald Trump, Massie said: "I think the president needs to see one of — this is a metaphor — one of his horses shot out from under him, and then maybe he'll he will see things differently.".

If the House does vote on Massie’s resolution, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is expected to become the House speaker in the next Congress, remarked on ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday that he would be a “hard yes” on it.

Sources indicate that hegseth has “got to go,” Jeffries noted. “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe.”.

Most if not all House Democrats are expected to agree.

Last week, Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the ranking member of the Armed Services Committee and its likely chairman in the next Congress, indicated in an interview with The New Republic that he would support Massie’s impeachment resolution, and he predicted it would be adopted.

According to recent reports, referring to Massie’s measure, Smith stated, “By every estimation, it will pass and he will be impeached. And off that goes to the Senate. Then the Senate is legally required to spend all of their time dealing with that until it’s done with.”.

In a recent development, "Every second Pete Hegseth remains at the top of the Pentagon, our servicemembers are at risk," Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., a senior member of the Armed Services Committee, remarked in a post on X on Sunday.

Recent findings suggest that also on Monday, Everett B. Kelley, the national president of the American Federation of Government Employees, a union that represents some 820,000 federal and D.C. government employees, sent a letter to House members urging a “yes” vote on Massie's Hegseth impeachment resolution.

The letter cited the risks Kelley noted the Iran war has posed to the lives of the Defense Department's uniformed and civilian personnel, and the missive noted Hegseth's stripping of workplace rights and protections for the department's civilians.

"By adopting Rep. Massie’s resolution, the House can begin the long overdue bipartisan effort to reclaim its constitutional powers and authority, restore checks and balances, and take responsibility for the lives of military personnel and civilian employees that Mr. Hegseth’s capricious leadership has jeopardized," Kelley wrote.

It has been revealed that massie announced in mid-September his intention to file an impeachment resolution against Hegseth. But Johnson adjourned the House before the vote would have occurred.

Massie’s upcoming resolution is substantially the same as his earlier one, with the same eight articles of impeachment.

The first three of these alleges that Hegseth’s conduct of the Iran war violated the War Powers Resolution.

Massie's measure notes Hegseth prosecuted the Iran war without congressional authorization and in the absence of an attack on the United States or an imminent threat.

According to recent reports, further, the measure alleges that Hegseth continued the war despite the House and Senate adopting in June a concurrent war powers resolution calling for the withdrawal of U.S. forces from the fight.

And, the resolution says, Hegseth continued the Iran war after the expiration of the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day termination period and any potential 30-day withdrawal period.

Massie’s measure further asserts that Hegseth:.

The House has only voted twice to impeach a member of the Cabinet. In 1876, Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached over allegations of corruption, and his abrupt resignation likely contributed to his acquittal in the Senate.

In 2024, the House voted 214-213 to impeach Alejandro Mayorkas, then-secretary of Homeland Security, for “willful and systemic refusal to comply with the law” and “breach of public trust.” The Senate dispensed with the charges without a trial.

#134394. Scientists may have found a way to track one of North America’s most elusive turtles

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1108 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists may have found a way to track one of North America’s most elusive turtles

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1108 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A tiny flatworm found in diamondback terrapins and the snails they eat may help scientists understand how turtle populations are connected.
  • Sources indicate that diamondback terrapins are hard to find and harder to count.
  • By reading this parasite’s genes along the US Atlantic coast, scientists found that its populations split into distinct groups.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A tiny flatworm found in diamondback terrapins and the snails they eat may help scientists understand how turtle populations are connected.

Sources indicate that diamondback terrapins are hard to find and harder to count. A latest study suggests that one of the best ways to follow them may be through a tiny flatworm that lives in their intestines and in the snails they eat.

By reading this parasite’s genes along the US Atlantic coast, scientists found that its populations split into distinct groups.

They also found a genetic dividing line about 300 kilometers south of where turtle experts had drawn the boundary between two terrapin subspecies.

The study was carried out by researchers from Florida Atlantic University’s Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute and East Carolina University.

Recent findings suggest that the diamondback terrapin is the only North American turtle that lives exclusively in brackish water, in salt marshes and estuaries along the coast. For a long time, people mostly ate it.

Turtle soup was a fashionable dish, and hunting for it drove the species into steep decline until the early 20th century. Then, in 1920, Prohibition banned sherry, a key ingredient in most turtle soup recipes.

Demand collapsed, and so did the hunting.

Sources indicate that that wasn’t a happy ending, though. Terrapins kept declining because of habitat loss, coastal development, and drowning in crab pots.

The species is now listed as “vulnerable” on the IUCN Red List. Conservationists want better data on where terrapin populations live and how they’re connected.

But the turtles are secretive and spread out, and catching enough to answer those questions is slow, expensive work.

The parasite is a fluke called Pleurogonius malaclemys. It can’t complete its life without two hosts.

Its eggs pass out in terrapin droppings and are eaten by eastern mudsnails. Inside the snail, the fluke multiplies by cloning itself.

Its larvae then leave the snail’s soft body and form small pearly cysts on the hard plate the snail uses to seal its shell.

When a terrapin eats an infected snail, the fluke grows into an adult in the turtle’s gut and reproduces sexually there.

According to recent reports, this arrangement is what makes the fluke useful. Mudsnails are abundant and easy to collect, and they barely move.

In a recent development, terrapins are the ones that carry the parasite from marsh to marsh. If the turtles don’t travel, the fluke’s genes don’t travel either. In principle, the parasite’s family tree should trace the turtle’s movements.

“One of the biggest challenges in conserving vulnerable species is understanding how populations are distributed and connected without having to capture and handle large numbers of animals,” said senior author Michael McCoy from FAU Harbor Branch.

“Our findings show that this parasite may provide an crucial window into the ecology of diamondback terrapins.”.

The team collected mudsnails from Cape Cod in Massachusetts to St. Augustine in Florida and dissected more than 4,000 of them. Infections inside the snails were rare, never reaching 4% at any site.

Recent findings suggest that the cysts outside were far more common, appearing on as many as 74% of snails at some marshes. Altogether, the fluke turned up at 23 of the 29 marshes sampled.

Finds on Cape Cod and in northeast Florida pushed its known range further north and south.

The Wetlands Institute provided the researchers with 38 female terrapins that had been killed by cars in Newly introduced Jersey.

Seventeen of them carried adult flukes, with up to seven worms per turtle.

According to recent reports, from 476 genetic sequences, the team found 102 distinct versions of a stretch of the fluke’s mitochondrial DNA. More than three-quarters of these versions turned up at only one location.

One version dominated the northern marshes, and another dominated the south. The farther apart two marshes were, the more their flukes differed genetically.

It has been revealed that that fits what is known about terrapins. The most mobile of them, adult females, have been recorded traveling no more than 8.5 kilometers. If the hosts stay close to home, their parasites become local too.

The most striking result was where the sharpest split fell. Biologists have traditionally drawn the line between the northern diamondback terrapin and the Carolina terrapin at Cape Hatteras in North Carolina.

The fluke’s genetic break falls instead between Wilmington, North Carolina, and Charleston, South Carolina, near the state border. That’s about 300 kilometers further south.

Terrapin subspecies were originally defined by their appearance, before genetic tools existed, so the parasite’s data adds to growing questions about where the real boundaries lie.

It has been revealed that the study also turned up something nobody had described before. Most fluke cysts are pearly white, but some had a faint blush or a pink ring around the edge, while others were bright fuchsia.

Sources indicate that they first appeared in North Carolina in 2023 and later in Massachusetts and Newly introduced Jersey, sometimes on the same snail as ordinary cysts. The color is in the cyst wall, not in the larva inside.

The pink cysts didn’t match any genetic group, and the researchers don’t yet know what causes them. One possibility is that they are simply older.

The authors make a broader point. Parasites account for nearly half of all known species, yet they are rarely studied and almost never protected.

It has been revealed that when a host declines, its parasites decline with it. Scientists recently formed an IUCN group dedicated to parasite conservation, and this study adds basic range and diversity data for a parasite that has been almost entirely ignored.

The team is careful not to overstate the results. The analysis used a single genetic marker, which is inherited only through the mother.

No one has yet compared fluke genetics directly with terrapin genetics from the same marshes, and that test will decide whether the fluke truly mirrors its host.

It has been revealed that counting cysts is also not a straightforward way to count turtles. One earlier study found that cyst numbers explained less than 8% of the variation in terrapin abundance.

“Our results point to an opportunity to look at conservation from a different perspective,” McCoy noted.

“Rather than relying exclusively on direct observations of terrapins, we can investigate the organisms that depend on them.”.

“Understanding where these parasites occur and how their populations are genetically connected could help scientists identify vital geographic divisions and develop better questions about how terrapin populations should be monitored and managed.”.

The study is published in the journal Ecology and Evolution.

In 1988, ice covered 1.66 square miles near the summit of Indonesia’s Puncak Jaya, and now what is left would fit on about a dozen soccer fields

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (816 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Landsat images show the ice near the summit of Puncak Jaya in Indonesia has dwindled to small patches that no longer flow like glaciers.
  • Sources indicate that in 1988, glaciers covered about 1.66 square miles (4.31 square kilometers) near the summit of Puncak Jaya, on the island of Fresh Guinea.
  • It has been revealed that that’s roughly 2 percent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Landsat images show the ice near the summit of Puncak Jaya in Indonesia has dwindled to small patches that no longer flow like glaciers.

Sources indicate that in 1988, glaciers covered about 1.66 square miles (4.31 square kilometers) near the summit of Puncak Jaya, on the island of Fresh Guinea. By September 2025, about 0.03 square miles (0.09 square kilometers) were left.

It has been revealed that that’s roughly 2 percent. What’s left would fit on about a dozen soccer fields.

It also no longer moves. The patches are too thin and too broken up to behave like a glacier, NASA Earth Observatory reported on November 16.

Puncak Jaya stands in the Sudirman Range, in the Indonesian part of New Guinea. Very few places this close to the equator have held ice all year round.

In a recent development, next door is the largest stretch of warm ocean water on the planet. So the glaciers here sit near the warmest conditions in which year-round ice can survive at all.

It has been revealed that scientists have called them high-altitude canaries in the coal mine. Other members of that small club are what’s left of Humboldt Glacier in Venezuela, the ice fields of Kilimanjaro in Tanzania and the Quelccaya Ice Cap in Peru, a country that has lost more than half of its glaciers in six decades.

NASA compared two false-color pictures of the range. Landsat 5 took one on November 3, 1988. Landsat 9 took the other on October 19, 2026.

Ice demonstrates up light blue, bare rock brown, clouds white and plants green. In 1988, blue caps several of the highest ridges. In 2026 there are only a few small blue fragments, and brown rock covers most of the old icy ridgetops.

Sources indicate that the area figures come from Donaldi Permana, a climate scientist at Indonesia’s Agency for Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics (BMKG). The 2025 number is based on satellite and aerial data.

An aerial survey is planned for December. It should show how much ice is left in 2026, Permana noted.

It has been revealed that the ice got thinner, too. At the main monitoring site, on the East Northwall Firn, it was 105 feet (32 meters) thick in 2010, Permana stated.

Industry observers note that in 2023 it measured 13 feet (4 meters). By November 2024 there was no ice there at all.

Thinning ice also cracks apart. Each newly introduced piece has fresh edges where it can melt, and so the losses feed on themselves.

It has been revealed that in the 2026 image, newly bared rock sits between the remnants. Snow still falls on the mountain. It just doesn’t stay on the bare rock long enough to turn into new ice.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s a house of cards problem,” mentioned Chris Shuman, a retired University of Maryland glaciologist who has followed Puncak Jaya’s glaciers in satellite images. “Once this process gets going, there’s really no turning back.”.

Recent findings suggest that to count as a glacier, a body of ice generally has to do two things. It has to be thick enough to creep downhill under its own weight. And it needs a zone where snow piles up faster than it melts.

On Puncak Jaya, the ice is now so thin, and so split into small, stagnant patches, that it has stopped flowing.

“While small ice remnants persist in high-altitude crevices around Puncak Jaya, their functional life as active glaciers is effectively over,” Permana noted.

El Niño years are especially rough on these glaciers. Warmer air pushes the freezing level above the summit, so rain falls instead of snow.

It has been revealed that fresh snow is white. It bounces sunlight away and protects the ice underneath. Without it, the darker surface soaks up heat and melts faster.

Sources indicate that during the 2015-2016 El Niño, the ice thinned about five times faster than normal, a finding NASA links to a study in PNAS. In one year it lost roughly 17 feet (5.3 meters) of thickness.

According to recent reports, then came the 2023-2024 El Niño. The ice thinned again, by about 7 to 13 feet (2 to 4 meters) a year.

Sources indicate that recent satellite studies suggest the main ice areas could be gone completely around 2030. For this, NASA links a study published in The Cryosphere.

BMKG’s own estimates suggest the ice could disappear much sooner, Permana noted, with the current El Niño speeding things up. Either way, Puncak Jaya’s ice looks set to vanish well before Africa’s remaining glaciers, which may be gone by 2040.

NASA links the 2 percent figure to a World Meteorological Organization report, State of the Climate in the South-West Pacific 2025.

The information was obtained from NASA Earth Observatory.

Swordfish hunt about 2,000 feet down, but every so often one plunges as deep as a mile, and scientists suspect it is reading the ocean

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1119 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Satellite tags on 34 North Atlantic swordfish caught rare dives past 3,280 feet.
  • Sources indicate that swordfish spend their days hunting in the dark, about 2,000 feet (600 meters) below the surface.
  • It has been revealed that satellite tags on North Atlantic swordfish have caught these rare plunges past 3,280 feet (1,000 meters).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Satellite tags on 34 North Atlantic swordfish caught rare dives past 3,280 feet. They were short and came near eddies and fronts, hinting the fish check the ocean.

Sources indicate that swordfish spend their days hunting in the dark, about 2,000 feet (600 meters) below the surface. Every so often, one keeps going.

It has been revealed that satellite tags on North Atlantic swordfish have caught these rare plunges past 3,280 feet (1,000 meters). Nobody knows why the fish make them.

A team from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) has now looked at years of tagging data in search of an answer. The dives were short, fairly steady, and most common where surface temperatures varied and the sea surface stood higher. The authors think the fish may be sampling the water column, possibly to help them find their way. The study was published in Marine Biology.

In a recent development, swordfish live in open oceans around the world, from about 45 degrees north to 45 degrees south. They follow a daily rhythm. By day they stay deep, usually between about 1,300 and 2,300 feet (400 and 700 meters), and at night they rise toward the surface.

Recent findings suggest that that routine follows their food. Huge numbers of small animals live in the ocean’s twilight zone and move up and down each day, and swordfish track them. Like other large predators of the open sea, tuna and swordfish get much of their food from that dim layer.

Sources indicate that swordfish can handle water from about 36 to 88 degrees Fahrenheit (2 to 31 degrees Celsius). They keep their eyes and parts of their body warmer than the surrounding water, which helps them stay deep for long periods.

It has been revealed that the researchers combined data from 34 pop-up satellite tags placed on North Atlantic swordfish between 2003 and 2024. Twenty-three were tagged off the Atlantic coast of Florida, six near the Grand Banks off Canada, three in the southern Sargasso Sea and two in the Gulf of America, also known as the Gulf of Mexico. Twenty-four were probably adults and 10 were probably juveniles.

Industry observers note that the tags stayed on for one to six months and logged depth, temperature and light. Together, they covered 3,666 days of swordfish life.

The data came from a partnership with NOAA’s Southeast Fisheries Science Center and the Massachusetts Division of Marine Fisheries.

“It wouldn’t have been possible to analyze this from just a single tagging operation, or from a single lab,” said Simon Thorrold, a fish ecologist at WHOI and an author of the study.

In a recent development, the team flagged 39 days on which a fish went unusually deep for its own normal pattern. On 25 of those days, recorded by 10 tags, the data were detailed enough to confirm a distinct extreme dive.

Recent findings suggest that these dives averaged about 3,250 feet (991 meters) at their deepest point, and the deepest reached roughly 5,460 feet (1,664 meters), more than a mile down. On ordinary days, the fish’s deepest point averaged about 2,090 feet (637 meters).

According to recent reports, A single extreme dive lasted about 45 to 55 minutes on average. When a fish made one such dive in a day, it usually dropped two to three times faster than it climbed back. In one fish’s full-resolution record, it spent between a few seconds and about six minutes at the bottom.

Recent findings suggest that the water at the bottom of these dives averaged about 47 degrees Fahrenheit (8.4 degrees Celsius). On other days, the coldest water the fish met averaged about 54 degrees Fahrenheit (12.1 degrees Celsius).

Most dives started and ended in the twilight zone, during daylight. In 12 of 16 such dives, the fish came back to within about 33 feet (10 meters) of the depth where it began.

The authors weighed seven possible reasons for deep dives, including feeding, escaping predators, saving energy and navigation.

According to recent reports, feeding seemed unlikely. A hunting fish would be expected to linger at depth, but these fish barely paused at the bottom before heading back up. The dives also did not cluster at dawn and dusk, when prey is easiest to reach.

It has been revealed that escape did not fit well either. The descents were steady, about 3.3 feet (1 meter) per second, and the fish behaved normally afterward. Only one dive began and ended near the surface at night, when the authors think predators may be more likely to be around. The authors could not rule out that the two juveniles, which made several dives in a single day, were avoiding predators.

It has been revealed that extreme dives were much more likely where sea surface temperature varied a lot and where the sea surface stood higher. In the team’s model, each extra degree Celsius of temperature variation made a dive about 23 times more likely. These conditions mark swirling eddies, fronts and major currents such as the Gulf Stream.

According to recent reports, the authors suggest that crossing into a new water mass may prompt a swordfish to check what lies below. Short, repeatable dives of the same shape would fit that kind of sampling.

“They could be coming into an ocean weather system, like an eddy or a frontal system, where we have a change in water masses,” mentioned Ciara Willis, who led the study as a doctoral student in the MIT-WHOI Joint Program and now works at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute.

Deeper water could also give a clearer reading of Earth’s magnetic field, which many fish can sense, away from the busy, changing layers near the surface. Some dives happened near seamounts, ridges and magnetic anomalies, but those links were weak, though rough seafloor indicated a smaller but significant effect. Other ocean travelers are under similar suspicion, as oceanic manta rays also dive deep, apparently not to feed.

It has been revealed that the authors stress that their conclusions are inferences. Satellite tag positions carry an average error of about 60 to 90 miles (100 to 150 kilometers), and possibly more for deep divers like swordfish. That makes it hard to match a dive to a specific seafloor feature.

It is still unclear how common these dives are among swordfish, and whether they differ between populations or ages.

Swordfish support valuable fisheries, so knowing what steers them could help predict where they go as the ocean changes.

The information was obtained from the study published in Marine Biology and from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.

#134389. Tech Report: A metal detectorist found a Viking sword and rare oval brooches on the Isle of Man, and his father had helped find the island’s only other pair

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (910 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: A metal detectorist found a Viking sword and rare oval brooches on the Isle of Man, and his father had helped find the island’s only other pair

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (910 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Daniel Crowe found a Viking sword, oval brooches and trading weights over 1,100 years old on the Isle of Man.
  • Recent findings suggest that A metal detectorist on the Isle of Man has found a Viking sword, a set of bronze brooches and trading weights and scales, all more than 1,100 years old.
  • Sources indicate that the finder, Daniel Crowe, is not the first in his family to make a discovery like this.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Daniel Crowe found a Viking sword, oval brooches and trading weights over 1,100 years old on the Isle of Man. His father helped find the island's only other pair.

Recent findings suggest that A metal detectorist on the Isle of Man has found a Viking sword, a set of bronze brooches and trading weights and scales, all more than 1,100 years old. The objects are believed to come from a double Viking burial.

Sources indicate that the finder, Daniel Crowe, is not the first in his family to make a discovery like this. In December 2018, his father, John Crowe, and fellow detectorist Craig Evans found the only other pair of Viking oval brooches ever discovered on the island.

The upcoming collection was declared Treasure by the Isle of Man Coroner for Inquests, and Manx National Heritage declared it on November 9. Part of it went on display at the Manx Museum in Douglas two days later.

According to recent reports, the finds date to around AD 900. Besides the sword, the haul includes three bronze brooches, decorated lead weights, fragments of bronze balance scales, a bronze ladle and an axehead.

In a recent development, fellow detectorist Rhett Britton helped with the search. He found the axehead, part of the scales and other iron objects.

According to recent reports, the sword is the thirteenth Viking sword found on the island. About two-thirds of it survives. X-rays revealed fine silver inlay and twisted silver wire on parts of its hilt, and only two other Manx Viking swords carry comparable decoration.

It is broken, probably on purpose as part of the burial ritual. Some more damage happened later, while it lay in the ground.

Two of the brooches are oval and decorated with interlocking animals, a distinctive feature of Viking art. Brooches like these were usually worn by women.

Recent findings suggest that the pair found by John Crowe and Craig Evans in 2018 dates to around AD 900 to 950. The latest pair could be about 50 years older, which would make it potential evidence of the earliest known female Viking Age burial on the Isle of Man.

Oval brooches were particularly common in the Viking homelands and are seen almost as national dress.

In 2020, Manx National Heritage noted their absence from the island until the 2018 find had led to theories that only men from Scandinavia settled there in the early Viking Age.

The third brooch was originally gilded. It has spiral decoration and a glass center, and it is the first of its kind found on the island.

Jewelry typically associated with women, found alongside a sword traditionally associated with men, raises a possibility. The objects may come from a double burial, or from separate graves of the same period.

The site was disturbed at some point over the last thousand years, so the exact circumstances are still uncertain.

At the site of the 2018 brooches, archaeologists from York Archaeological Trust carried out a small excavation but found no grave.

The decorated lead weights and bronze scales would have been used to weigh precious metals and coins during trade. The weights are the first of their type found on the Isle of Man.

Silver and coins also turn up in hoards across the Viking world, like a buried 10th-century hoard that revealed vast Viking trade networks.

Industry observers note that one weight carries a bronze fitting, possibly taken from a small chest or a religious object. Its art style is typical of Britain and Ireland at the time, which suggests the settlers reused objects from other cultures.

The ladle, perhaps used at feasts or ceremonies, is another type of object never recorded before on the island.

“This is an extraordinary discovery and one of the most significant groups of Viking Age objects found on the Isle of Man,” said Allison Fox, Curator for Archaeology at Manx National Heritage.

Crowe chose not to clean the objects and handed them over in the state they came out of the ground. That kept traces of evidence that could otherwise have been lost.

His father and Evans did the same in 2018. In 2020, Fox mentioned this mattered because the brooches were fragile and small fragments of textiles from the clothes the woman was buried in might still survive.

Industry observers note that this time, before conservation began, the radiology team at Manx Care scanned the objects. The scans looked beneath layers of compacted soil and guided the conservator in uncovering and preserving the objects.

Detectorists elsewhere have made similar finds, such as the hiker with a metal detector who found a Viking treasure hoard and the detectorist who found Finland’s largest Viking Age silver hoard.

Manx National Heritage has not said exactly where the objects were found, only that the landowner cooperated. It also has not given a date for the discovery.

Recent findings suggest that conservation and research are still underway, and they may reveal more about who owned these objects. Several of them are the first of their kind on the island, so they offer a rare look at early Viking settlement, burial and daily life there.

Visitors can see a selection of the finds in the Viking Gallery of the Manx Museum.

The information was obtained from Manx National Heritage and its 2020 announcement on the earlier brooches.

Breaking: November’s full moon on Nov. 24 is the first of three supermoons in a row, and it will pass close to the Pleiades

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The November 24, 2026 Beaver Moon will be the first of three consecutive supermoons, with views of the Pleiades, Mars and Jupiter before dawn.
  • The full Moon of November 24, 2026, will be a supermoon, the first of three consecutive supermoons that run through January.
  • Industry observers note that the Moon turns full at 9:53 a.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The November 24, 2026 Beaver Moon will be the first of three consecutive supermoons, with views of the Pleiades, Mars and Jupiter before dawn.

The full Moon of November 24, 2026, will be a supermoon, the first of three consecutive supermoons that run through January.

Industry observers note that the Moon turns full at 9:53 a.m. EST (14:53 UT), the U.S. Naval Observatory calculates. That is midmorning on the East Coast, so the best views come before dawn and again that evening.

Before sunrise, the nearly full Moon will pass close to the Pleiades star cluster, while Mars and Jupiter shine in another part of the sky.

Recent findings suggest that the Moon’s orbit is slightly oval, so its distance from Earth changes. At its closest point, called perigee, it is about 226,000 miles (363,300 kilometers) away, and at its farthest about 251,000 miles (405,500 kilometers).

According to recent reports, A supermoon occurs when a full Moon coincides with that closest approach, NASA explains. The word is not an official astronomical term and typically describes a full Moon within at least 90 percent of perigee.

Such a Moon can appear up to 14 percent bigger and 30 percent brighter than the faintest full Moon of the year.

According to recent reports, “It might be hard to detect a supermoon visually, but it does have an effect on Earth,” the space agency’s page states. A Moon at perigee can cause higher tides than usual.

Measured against an average full Moon, the gain is smaller: up to 7 percent larger and 15 percent brighter, the Royal Observatory Greenwich notes.

When it turns full, the Moon will be roughly 224,200 miles (360,800 kilometers) from Earth. That is around 12,400 miles (20,000 kilometers) closer than average, by the Greenwich astronomers’ figures.

According to recent reports, perigee itself arrives about 30 hours later, on November 25 at 4:01 p.m. EST. The Moon will then be 223,400 miles (359,567 kilometers) away, a government almanac from Land Information New Zealand reveals.

In a recent development, december’s full Moon falls on December 23 at 8:28 p.m. EST. Perigee follows about seven hours later at 221,800 miles (356,903 kilometers), the closest of the three.

The third full Moon comes on January 22, 2027, at 7:17 a.m. EST. Perigee occurs the previous afternoon, at 222,200 miles (357,530 kilometers).

According to recent reports, measured at perigee, November’s supermoon is therefore the most distant of the trio. It follows the Beaver Moon of November 2025.

U.S. Naval Observatory rise and set tables put moonset in Fresh York at 7:05 a.m. EST, 12 minutes after sunrise. In Los Angeles, the Moon sets at 6:49 a.m. PST.

Early risers should look low in the west, toward Taurus, the constellation that holds the Pleiades.

The International Occultation Timing Association lists that date among the Moon’s 2026 passages over the cluster. In an occultation, the Moon moves in front of a star and hides it.

The listing does not rank it among the year’s best passages. Bright moonlight will also make the cluster’s faint stars harder to pick out.

In a recent development, higher up, Mars and Jupiter have been neighbors all month. They appeared about 1.2 degrees apart on the mornings of November 15 and 16, slightly more than two full Moon widths.

Jupiter is the brighter of the two, and Mars has a reddish tint. Binoculars or a low-powered telescope, under 40x magnification, give a closer look.

The planets have since drifted apart and stand high in the south before dawn, near Regulus, the brightest star in Leo.

Recent findings suggest that such Mars and Jupiter pairings recur every 2 to 2.5 years on average, by the Royal Observatory’s count. Mars circles the Sun faster and laps Jupiter in the night sky.

The second chance comes at dusk. “Look east around sunset to watch it rise,” NASA’s November skywatching guide advises.

According to recent reports, “It may look even bigger near the horizon, but that’s the Moon illusion,” the guide adds. The effect is common to any full Moon.

Moonrise in Latest York is at 4:16 p.m. EST, 16 minutes before sunset. Los Angeles sees the Moon come up at 4:43 p.m. PST, two minutes ahead of the Sun’s setting.

Bill Ingalls, then NASA’s senior photographer, shared supermoon photography tips in 2016.

“Don’t make the mistake of photographing the moon by itself with no reference to anything,” Ingalls said. “I’ve certainly done it myself, but everyone will get that shot.”.

He suggested including a local landmark to give a photo a sense of place. For phone cameras, he advised holding a finger on the Moon to lock focus, then sliding it to adjust exposure.

According to recent reports, beaver Moon is a nickname for November’s full Moon. The name draws on several traditions and folklore in Native American and European culture.

One explanation is that beavers spend November fortifying their dams and stocking food for winter. The month was also the season to trap the animals for their thick, winter-ready pelts.

“There is disagreement over the origin of November’s ‘Beaver Moon’ name,” the Royal Observatory’s monthly highlights state.

The word “supermoon” was coined in 1979, the same 2024 NASA post states.

The information was obtained from NASA’s skywatching guide.

The 6 Best Metal Detectors for Treasure Hunters and Experts Alike

📅 28 Jun 2020 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3068 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

💡 Key Takeaways

It's easy to fantasize about stumbling upon a hoard of buried pirate gold or, more realistically, a lost piece of jewelry, but the reality of metal detecting is this: It's more about the process of searching than the actual find itself.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

You've probably seen a metal detectorist hard at work at a beach or park with their funky-looking gadget and thought, "I wish I had one of those." It's easy to fantasize about stumbling upon a hoard of buried pirate gold or, more realistically, a lost piece of jewelry, but the reality of metal detecting is this: It's more about the process of searching than the actual find itself.

According to recent reports, that stated, metal detecting can be a fun and relaxing hobby for anyone to try, especially with friends, and the barrier to entry is low. It’s an activity that gives you an excuse to spend a few hours outside, scouring the sand or dirt for coins or who-knows-what, and you might even find something that really makes it worth your while, though it's best if you don't expect to.

Industry observers note that to determine the best metal detectors for newbies and experts alike, I tested a number of different models on the beaches and in the parks of South Florida, rating their performance, handling, and overall usability across several different terrains. I also consulted with an expert detectorist who helped me understand what factors to consider when making my choices. No matter which of these machines works best for your use case, all of them are great gets.

I selected the best metal detectors after trying a handful of options that came recommended to me by Jeff Lubbert, an expert detectorist who has been tracking down treasures and finding lost rings since the mid-1980s, and a handful of other expert detectorists.

According to recent reports, lubbert has used his metal detector in 28 states, one United States territory, five foreign countries, and three foreign territories, where he has recovered items adding up to approximately $980,000. He is president of the Eureka Treasure Hunters Club in Denver, Colorado, and has written articles about metal detectors for outlets like American Diggers. He's also appeared on the TV show Forensic Files.

To test accuracy, I buried an old spoon and two different coins—a quarter and a penny—8 inches underground to check their level of discrimination and pinpointing. I also used each detector for several hours in a variety of conditions, including in a grassy park and at the beach, in both dry sand and wet sand, and under several inches of surf.

The Minelab Vanquish 560 is a dynamic metal detector that works well on every terrain, including wet sand, and is incredibly intuitive to use. Unlike the slightly cheaper Vanquish 440, my previous top recommendation, the 560 is waterproof to 16 feet, which makes it suitable for wading and underwater use. It also includes a rechargeable battery, a flashlight, and Bluetooth headphone support, making it one of the most fully-featured detectors in this guide, and especially for this price.

While it only has four find modes (including an adjustable “custom” option). That’s are far fewer than you will find on professional-grade detectors like the Minelab Equinox 900, but it's still much more than enough for most amateur metal detectorists.

The Vanquish 560 punches well above its weight, and value-wise, it's the best detector we tested on a per-dollar basis. It may feel like a splurge for first-timers, but you’re getting what you pay for. And it’s an incredibly handsome upgrade for folks looking strong accuracy and some quality-of-life improvements.

In a recent development, since I primarily spoke with experts and enthusiasts, the Nokta FindX Pro was not remotely on my radar when I first began my research. But it may just be the best option for upcoming detectorists looking to dip a toe into the hobbyist pool. It’s an all-in-one kit, complete with an effective digging tool, a nice duffel bag, and decent headphones—all for less than $200.

Recent findings suggest that while it is not as accurate as my other recommendations, it’s a more than capable VLF detector. I was able to find items at both parks and beaches, though I noticed that its performance really suffered on wet sand and underwater. Its compact frame and adjustable handle make it accommodating to a wider-than-average range of newcomers, including kids and adults.

If you’re interested in the hobby and don’t want to spend too much to try it, the FindX Pro is a great fit for beginners.

According to recent reports, while I wasn’t able to get this detector in for my current round of tests, Lubbert recommended the Minelab Manticore for expert detectorists who want the ultimate metal detector experience. He notes it can visualize the ground beneath it in a 2D map, directing you to finds with depths and ID targets. It should work well in any terrain, including underwater, and has the most advanced backlight of any Minelab machine. Plus, with 10 search modes, there are many options for veteran detectorists looking to optimize for a specific type of search.

The price is substantial, but if you’re willing to spend this much money on a detector, I’m confident that it will be worth it.

Industry observers note that the Simplex line is often recommended by experts as a good entry point for upcoming detectorists. Nokta is one of the two biggest brands in the metal detecting game—the other is Minelab—and the Simplex Lite is a strong, basic VLF detector. I found it had top-notch discrimination, plenty of find modes, and a good coil size that easily found my testing materials and led me to beer cans, aluminum foil, and plenty of other objects on the beach.

Because this is a single-frequency VLF detector, it doesn’t perform as well as the Vanquish 440, especially on the mineralized sand at saltwater beaches. It’s still a very capable machine, though—even more so if you’re searching for a specific type of item, particularly coins and jewelry. Though it offers fewer customization options than its more expensive multi-frequency counterparts, it’s also much easier to pick up and use as a newcomer.

For those who are looking to spend a bit more, you can upgrade to the Simplex Ultra, which adds Bluetooth support and gives you precision detector tools like target ID scale and depth.

Recent findings suggest that underwater metal detecting is typically the domain of serious enthusiasts, especially if it’s in seawater. If this sounds intriguing, two different experts for metal detector recommendations (including Lubbert) suggest the XP Deus II, a high-end machine that specializes in just that. Expert Stanley Ross, known as the Metal Detector Man, who we spoke with for this article previously, says that he uses his Deus II to search for lost rings and other jewelry on the beach all the time.

Sources indicate that the Deus II has something called "fast multi-frequency" technology, which allows for superior multi-frequency detection in a variety of conditions, and it's rated for up to 20 meters of water, a massive upgrade compared to our other picks that top out at 5 meters of water resistance. Our other multi-frequency picks use similar technology, but the Deus II offers better and faster response in saltwater conditions, making it easier to pinpoint buried targets without having to pass over the same spot multiple times, especially underwater.In order to use the Deus II underwater, however, you'll need a few accessories, including its waterproof wireless headphones and an underwater remote control. While these upgrades are technically “optional” in the sense that you can easily use the Deus II on land without them, they are virtually required for anything beyond getting your ankles wet.

Both of these additions will increase the price of the overall package considerably, depending on which exact model of headphones you choose. Both the $280 WS6 headphones (which can control the detector, but are not recommended for underwater use) and the $749 remote control have slightly different interfaces, but the remote control is generally recommended for both ease of use and underwater functionality. Because of its high customizability and 12 preset modes, the Deus II isn't quite as beginner-friendly as some of our other picks.

While I haven't yet tested the Deus II for myself, it’s highly regarded among enthusiasts. If you're interested in underwater detecting—whether that's wading around or even diving down—this choice will not disappoint.

The Minelab Equinox 900 is the most feature-rich metal detector I tested. From the second I picked it up, I could tell that it would be a cut above the rest. The build quality is noticeably better than that of other, less expensive models I tested—it just feels more substantial.

Its features and performance back up that first impression. The Equinox 900 consistently performed better than its less expensive counterparts as well, pinpointing targets precisely and identifying both their depth and target ID. Though I was able to find my planted targets with every detector, the Equinox 900 directed me precisely to all three, making the process quicker and easier in both dry and wet sand.

It also features a number of settings and tools that improve the detecting experience, including six customizable frequency settings, an easy-adjust handle, and Bluetooth support so you can use wireless headphones. All that customization is incredible if you’re an expert. I personally had more success using the premade settings, but I can see detectorists like Lubbert fine-tuning searches to great effect.

I was especially taken with its handgrip vibration feature, which gives you a rumbling haptic response when the Equinox picks up a target. It’s a great way to get your attention in a loud area, if you’re hearing-impaired, or if you’re just on a long walk and not paying close attention. Personally, I found it very helpful while roaming some very popular stretches of Miami’s beaches.

It’s worth noting that Minelab lists the Equinox 900 as a bit heavier than the other models we tested, though I personally didn’t notice a difference, even after several hours of sweeping. At more than triple the price of my best overall pick, it’s fair to say that the Equinox 900 is an investment for serious hobbyists. But it is far and away the most effective choice I tested and a worthy upgrade.

In addition to a decent pair of headphones, it helps to carry a pinpointer when using your metal detector. These precise, short-range auxiliary detectors assist you with determining the exact location of a find after picking something up with your detector’s large coil.

In a recent development, this one, from Minelab, is relatively expensive, but fully waterproof with five sensitivity levels, and it works very well. It also features ferrous discrimination, which allows it to tell if a target is made of ferrous metals like iron or non-ferrous metals like gold, silver, or copper. It isn’t strictly necessary but is an extra feature you’ll enjoy using in trash-filled parks.

We tested and loved the Minelab Vanquish 440, a slightly cheaper version of our current best overall pick, the Vanquish 560. It was recently replaced with a new and improved model, the Minelab Vanquish 460, which is also a strong choice. We ultimately chose to recommend the 560 because it offers a more robust set of features and works well over more types of terrain.

While shopping for a metal detector, you need to take into account a number of key factors, particularly the type, coil size, weight, and extra features like backlight and frequency customization. Weight and build quality also make a massive difference, especially when you use these devices for hours at a time. It was initially hard to weigh these distinct traits, but after testing these machines myself, the features worth springing for became clear.

If you’re going to shop for a hobby-grade metal detector, it’s key to understand how they work. This is fairly technical equipment, so manufacturers will cater their products primarily to veterans who already have a bit of knowledge, which may be intimidating to fresh people.

Most metal detectors have a round head called the “search coil,” which is the actual detector itself. It has two parts, the transmitter coil and the receiver coil, which work in tandem to produce an electromagnetic field that shoots down into the ground wherever you wave it. When the field hits metal, it triggers another magnetic effect in response, which the coil picks up. Depending on the device, that signal may be able to tell you how deep an object is buried, based on the strength of the response.

Industry observers note that most of the detectors I recommend can determine what kind of metal they’re reading by measuring the object’s “phase shift,” or the time it takes for the object to react when the coil changes its magnetic current. This function, called “discrimination,” can sometimes help you figure out if your quarry is worth digging up before you go to the trouble of getting your digging tools out. However, as Lubbert notes, discrimination is not always reliable, and it’s generally best to err on the side of digging if you think you’ve found something worthwhile.

The first thing to look at before buying a metal detector is where you plan to use it, as some detectors are better equipped to scan specific types of terrain. For example, if you live near the coast and plan to sweep your local beach, you may want a different model than someone looking under hard soil in local parks. Though there are many kinds of detectors, I focused on the two most frequently used by novices and veteran hobbyists.

The physical size of the metal detector coil is important, too. If you don’t sweep the coil over an object, you aren’t going to get a ping, so bigger is better. Under most conditions, Lubbert recommends looking for a coil that’s at least 11 inches in diameter.

According to recent reports, that remarked, Lubbert advises that smaller coils have their uses, especially in wooded areas, since it’s easier to get between twigs, grass, and weeds with a more compact head. Larger coils can theoretically detect objects that are deeper underground, but they’re also more susceptible to electromagnetic interference from the environment. He recommends having both a compact coil and a large coil option if you initiative to scan a wide range of environments.

Recent findings suggest that in general, all of my recommendations here seem relatively light on paper—the heaviest weighs only a few pounds. Keep in mind, though, that you could be waving this device around with one arm for hours at a time. Even a few ounces can greatly impact how quickly you tire out.

Mid-range and high-end metal detectors tend to feature backlit displays, which come in handy when searching in low-light conditions. (Some high-end models even come with flashlight functions). Though not a universal feature, I consider this essential for all but the cheapest options.

Industry observers note that high-end metal detectors grant you a degree of customization through advanced settings, allowing you to set a specific level of discrimination that, when properly used, can help you identify relics and coins in a variety of environments. You need to know what you’re doing to take full advantage of these do-it-yourself search modes, but there are guides online to help you learn as you go.

It has been revealed that lastly, most metal detectors I researched and/or tested feature built-in batteries that last for hours on a full charge. That said, some models—including one of my picks—use disposable batteries instead. There are advantages and disadvantages to both: Disposable batteries can be replaced quickly, but you need to keep spare cells on you. It comes down to your preference, so go with what feels right.

“Make each swing of the detector take about 2 seconds and overlap your swings so that the coil covers all of the ground,” Lubbert states. “Wear headphones, as it helps you hear those deep target whispers.”.

According to recent reports, lubbert also mentioned that detectorists should be happy with what they find, and that you should expect 95 percent of your digs to result in trash. When that happens, be cool, and make sure to dispose of it properly.

According to Lubbert, a dedicated detectorist should have a pinpointer, proper recovery tools like a shovel, and a pouch to store trash and treasure separately.

Based on my testing experience and to echo his point above, I found headphones to be a must-have when using a metal detector, as the built-in speakers are difficult to hear, especially on a crowded beach.

Industry observers note that finding a legal place to use your metal detector is not as easy as you might think. It’s illegal to use a detector in U.S. National Parks and historic battlefields. Many cities ban using them on public property or require you to apply for a permit beforehand. Make sure to check your local city and county laws to determine if and where you may be allowed to use a metal detector and if you’ll need a permit to do so.

And, of course, if you proposal to use your detector on private property, you should obtain permission from the owner, or else you might dig up a lawsuit instead of treasure.

Steven T. Wright is a freelance writer based in Miami, FL. He has been a full-time writer of various things for around a decade, especially long-form features about tech and digital culture. He enjoys spending time with his wife and cat, hiking, and reading weird fiction. You can follow him on Twitter @MadCathedral.

Jeff Lubbert has been an avid metal detector since 1980 and joined The Ring Finders directory in 2010. He is an active officeholder in Denver's Eureka Treasure Hunters Club and the co-host of American Digger Magazine's Relic Roundup, a weekly metal detecting podcast.

How the ‘blue tsunami’ crested in North Carolina
